title: How Does a Snail Move on Just 1 Foot? 🐌
description:
How do snails move on one foot? Waves of muscle ripple along a snail's foot while its slime acts as glue under the still parts and turns runny where a wave pushes, so the snail slides forward at roughly a millimetre a second.

Sources:
https://www.nature.com/articles/285160a0
https://www.popsci.com/environment/why-snail-slug-slow/
https://scienceinsights.org/how-fast-can-a-snail-travel-the-science-explained/

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

topic: How does a snail crawl on just one foot?
script:
A snail never lifts its one foot.
Can you guess how it moves?
Put a snail on glass and look underneath.
Dark stripes ripple along the sole,
from the tail toward the head.
Those are waves of muscle,
squeezing and stretching the foot.
But the real trick is the slime.
Under the still parts of the foot,
it's thick and sticky, like glue.
Where a wave pushes on it,
it turns runny and slippery.
So each wave slides forward on liquid,
while the rest stays stuck down.
Glue, slide, glue, slide.
That grip lets a snail climb straight up a stem,
or hang under a leaf.
The catch? It's slow.
Roughly one millimetre a second.
So would you trade your two feet
for one slimy one?
key_facts: Snails crawl on one muscular foot; waves of muscle contraction (pedal waves) ripple along the sole, tail to head (Conversation/PopSci; ScienceInsights)
Pedal mucus acts as a glue for adhesion, and shear-thins to flow where a wave passes, then re-gels (Denny 1980, Nature; ScienceInsights)
Adhesion lets snails resist gravity on plants (Denny 1980)
A common garden snail moves roughly 1 mm per second (ScienceInsights; sources vary)
